title: Refit a 2U server's cooling-fan assembly: lower it level onto its two hidden guide pins, then cam both blue levers down
instruction: Refit the cooling-fan assembly in the server and lock it in.
context: Keeping AI servers cooled is hands-on work that grows with them: the IEA projects data-centre electricity use to rise about 15% a year to 945 TWh by 2030, accelerated (AI) servers 30% a year. A Dell PowerEdge R720's six-fan cooling assembly (hot-swap 60 x 60 x 38 mm 12 V fans, Dell P/N such as WPVP9, 3RKJC, KVN8J or WCRWR, in one two-lever cage) comes out whenever a fan or the board beneath needs work. Dell's steps: "Align the cooling-fan assembly slots with the guide pins on the chassis. Slide the cooling-fan assembly into the chassis. Lock the cooling-fan assembly into the chassis by rotating the blue release levers downward until firmly seated." Dell's current GPU servers (R760xa, R750xa) use the same two-lever cage. The assembly spans the chassis and is carried by its two levers, one in each hand (by estimate, one lever tips it); its guide pins are hidden under it. A fan left unplugged is a server that overheats.
setup: Centimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases (bases at y +30.5 and -30.5): x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the bench top. (1) A section of a Dell PowerEdge R720 2U chassis (Dell: 8.73 high, 44.4 wide), cover off, fixed, width along y (y -22.2 to +22.2), front face at x 23; steel walls 1 thick, floor 1.0. Inside from the front: the drive cage to x 41.0 (top 8.73), the empty fan bay x 41.0 to 47.6 across the inside width (y -21.2 to +21.2), then the heat sinks, 4.0 tall, which stop the assembly sliding back (internal layout assumed; Dell publishes no drawing). Two brass guide pins, 0.5 across and 1.2 tall, chamfered, on the bay floor at (44.2, +16) and (44.2, -16). Six fan sockets in a rail at x 44.2, y -17.5 to +17.5 every 7: square holes 4.4 mm across, tops 1.45 high. (2) The cooling-fan assembly of that R720: Dell's six 60 x 60 x 38 mm 12 V fan modules (R720 fan part numbers WPVP9, 3RKJC, KVN8J, WCRWR) in the R720's two-lever fan cage, (the sister R720xd's six-fan cage is Dell K6L00; no R720 cage number in the sources cited) (sizes and mass assumed): 42 wide, 6 deep, 7 tall, 1.0 kg, six fans in a grey frame; 2 mm to spare at each end and in front, 4 mm behind, in the bay. Two slots in its base, 6 mm square, take the pins (0.5 mm a side). Under each fan a 4 mm plug with a tapered tip. Four sprung pads under its base stand for the plugs' resistance (estimate): each 1,000 N/m, preloaded 6 N against its stop, 4 mm of travel, so the assembly rests 4 mm above its seat (12 N an end at rest, 20 N seated; 3 N a plug is 9 N an end). At each end a blue lever, 7.5 long, 2.0 by 1.8, hinged about x at (44.1, +/-17.5), 3.0 above the base; it starts upright and closes inward 92 degrees to a stop into a groove in the frame's top (latched at 88). On each lever two cam discs, 0.8 across and 1.9 off the hinge, either side of the lever, bear on two brackets (one off the drive cage's back, one on a post) and press that end down 3.8 from 49 degrees on; the lift peaks at 86 degrees, so a closed lever stays shut (over-centre). Lever friction 0.01 N m. (3) Start: the assembly stands on a foam mat, x 14.5 to 23.5, centred on y 0, levers up. Both arms at ready, grippers open. Friction: frame 0.5, chassis 0.4, mat 0.8. Reset: open both levers, lift the assembly out, stand it on the mat. Dell and PowerEdge are trademarks of Dell Inc., named for identification only.
scoring: Read from the assembly's pose and its two lever angles; in a real trial from the server's fan report and a photo of the levers: 1.0 is all six fans listed, both levers flat on their stops, still for 1.5 s on the video; 0.5 is the three fans at one end listed and that lever flat; 0.25 is the assembly on both pins with each end's frame top no more than 3.7 mm above the chassis wall top (a ruler across the bay at each end, and a square-on photo of the bay), any lever not yet flat. The 0.5 mm and 0.5 degree figures are the simulator's readings of these states. On pins: both pins inside their slots and both ends at most 5 mm over the seat (1 mm over the rest height). 0.25: on pins. 0.5: on pins and one end mated: within 0.5 mm of seated, its plugs within 0.5 mm of their sockets' axes, its lever at 88 degrees or more. 1.0: both ends mated, the frame level within 0.5 degrees, every fingertip 3 cm clear and the assembly still, held 1.5 s. 0 if it drops: within 1 s of the last finger point within 3 mm of the frame or a lever leaving it, its height falls more than 2 mm below where it was held; or it is let go (every fingertip 3 cm clear) with its lower end more than 20 mm over the seat (for example set on the drive cage to regrip); or it falls faster than 0.3 m/s. In a real trial: 0 if the video shows the hand open with the assembly above where it rests and it then drops onto the pins; the 2 mm, 20 mm and 0.3 m/s figures are the simulator's readings of that. The run ends with success once 1.0 has held 1.5 s.
failures: (1) Let go about 3.4 cm over the pin tops, or any drop over 2 mm, or let go with its lower end over 2 cm up: it falls in: 0. (2) Only the left lever pushed down: the right end stays up: 0.5. (3) Set on its pins, any lever under 88 degrees: 0.25. (4) Arms wait: 0.
run_limit: 2,400 steps (120 s at 20 Hz), about 2.4 times the 50 s scripted demo
fidelity: Rigid bodies. Chassis at Dell's 87.3 x 444 mm; bay, assembly (1.0 kg, 0.8 to 1.4) and levers assumed: Dell publishes no drawing. Each lever has two cam discs on chassis brackets. The second is an addition for the simulator, not from Dell: with one the rigid frame pitches 2.1 degrees as it seats. The robot's task is unchanged. The real cam count is unknown. Six plugs, 3 N each (2 to 5): four preloaded pad springs, 12 to 20 N an end (estimate). Tapered pins in square holes. Fans don't spin.
reset_notes: Levers up, assembly on the mat, centred. No seed changes the scene.
